notes.meaning: King Lemuel passes on a weighty message that his mother taught him. Many older teachers believed Lemuel was a loving name for Solomon. The name means 'belonging to God,' and they took his mother to be Bathsheba. Henry adds that mothers, not only fathers, should teach their children what is good.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars think Lemuel was a king outside Israel, perhaps 'king of Massa,' an Arabian people. They see no real evidence that he was Solomon.

notes.meaning: The repeated 'What?' shows a mother's deep, earnest love. It is as if her heart is full and she hardly knows where to begin. 'Son of my womb' means 'my very own son.' 'Son of my vows' means a son she prayed for and gave to God, much as Hannah did with Samuel.

She warns her son not to waste his strength of body and mind on women. That kind of living has ruined many kings, and even David fell badly in the matter of Uriah. Henry notes that ordinary people should take the same warning to heart.

Kings and rulers must not give themselves to wine or crave strong drink. A drunk ruler forgets the laws he is meant to keep. He then twists justice for the poor, when he should be helping them. People who judge others need clear heads, and Henry applies this to every Christian too.

differ.view: The warning is against drinking too much or needing drink. A total ban on wine would have been unheard of in an ancient royal court.
The verse forbids drinking wine at all, not just drinking too much. It applies to ordinary believers as well as kings.

notes.meaning: Strong drink should go to those who are dying or crushed with sorrow, not to kings. It can ease their pain and help them bear their trouble for a while. Wine is for real need, like medicine, not for pleasure, so the well-off should share it with those who suffer. Later, Jewish women gave such a drink to condemned prisoners. Jesus refused it on the cross so He could face death fully aware.

differ.view: Read with verse 4, this verse limits wine to those who are 'ready to perish' and to no one else.

notes.meaning: The king must speak up for people who cannot speak for themselves. Some are too weak, too afraid, too poor or too untaught to defend themselves in court. He is to judge fairly and stand up for the poor and needy like a lawyer on their side. A good ruler uses his power to protect the helpless.

These closing verses form an ABC poem: each verse starts with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet. 'Noble character' means 'a woman of strength,' made strong by wisdom, grace and the fear of God. Such a woman is rare and worth more than jewels. A man looking for a wife should look for character, not beauty or money. Some older writers also saw in her a picture of the church, the bride of Christ.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars see her mainly as a picture of Wisdom herself, praised like a war hero. On this view the poem sets a pattern for men as well as women.

notes.meaning: Her husband trusts her completely: her faithfulness, her judgment and her care for the family. Because she manages so well, he lacks nothing and never needs to make money by dishonest means. She does him good and not harm every day of her life. Her kindness is steady, not just when she is in a good mood.

She looks for good wool and flax (a plant used to make linen) and works with willing hands. The Hebrew pictures her working with 'the delight of her hands,' because she enjoys it. Her example also encourages her servants to work. Wesley adds that everyone, great or small, should use their time well for God.
Like trading ships, she looks beyond her own doorstep. She trades what she makes for good things from far away. She goes as far as she needs to so her household is well supplied.

She gets up before dawn to prepare food for her family and her servants. She also gives the servants their share of food and the day's tasks, so everything runs in good order. She puts care for her home ahead of her own comfort.

She thinks carefully before she buys a field, weighing whether it is worth the price and whether she can afford it. She plants a vineyard with money she has earned herself, not by going into debt. Henry notes that many people ruin themselves by buying without thinking first.
'Girds herself' pictures tucking up a long robe so you are ready to work, like rolling up your sleeves. She puts all her energy into her tasks and does not shy away from hard work.
She can see that her work pays off, and that spurs her on. Her lamp burning late at night is a picture of her tireless care. She makes good use of the evening hours.

The distaff and spindle are simple old tools for spinning thread. The distaff holds the wool or flax, and the spindle twists it into thread. Though she is well-off, she does this humble work with her own hands and sets an example for others.

She is as eager to give as she is to earn. She reaches out to the poor near her and to the needy farther away, freely and warmly. Keil and Delitzsch note that without this care for the suffering, she might please her husband but not God.

When cold weather comes, she does not worry, because she has already made warm clothes for everyone. Scarlet points to good woollen cloth that is warm and also looks fine. Some older translations read it as 'double clothing,' meaning extra layers for winter.

She makes fine coverings for her beds and home. Her own clothes are linen and purple, which were costly and fitting for a woman of her standing. She dresses well but does not make clothes the center of her life.

Her husband is respected at the city gate, where the town's leaders met to decide matters and judge cases. Part of his good name comes from her. Her wise care of the home frees him to serve the community.

She makes linen garments and sashes and sells them to traders. The word for 'merchants' literally means 'Canaanites,' that is, the Phoenician traders of the coast. She makes more than her family needs and sells the rest.

After describing her clothes, the poem describes the clothing of her spirit: strength and honor. She can laugh at the days ahead because she has prepared well and trusts in God's care. Henry adds that she can look back with joy in old age, and forward to joy forever.
When she speaks, her words are wise, and kindness rules her tongue. She gives helpful advice gently, like a friend, not like a boss. The Geneva Notes add that she loves to talk about God's word.

She keeps a close eye on everything in her home, including how her children and servants behave. 'The bread of idleness' means food you have not worked for. Even though she is well-off, she never lives lazily.

Her children rise up and call her blessed, giving her honor as the fifth commandment asks. Her husband praises her too: many women have done well, but she surpasses them all. Henry says it is right and loving for husbands and wives to praise each other.

Charm can fool people, and beauty soon fades with sickness, age and death. But a woman who fears the LORD, meaning she deeply respects God and lets Him guide all she does, deserves praise. This faith crowns everything else about her and is the lasting beauty of the soul. The book ends where it began, with the fear of the LORD.

Give her the reward she has earned, and let her deeds praise her in public. Even if people stay silent, her works speak for her, as the garments Dorcas made spoke for her in Acts 9. A truly good woman does not chase compliments; she lets her life do the talking.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Gregory the Great read 'the gates' in a spiritual way, as the day of judgment that opens into God's kingdom.
